title: Ukrainian robots change how army endures war, not just save lives
excerpt: Ukrainian commanders said one of the benefits of the robots is their ability to increase Kyiv's "operational endurance."
content_html:
Ukraine’s ground robots aren’t just saving lives — they’re changing the way its army endures the fight

By Jake Epstein

You're currently following this author! Want to unfollow? Unsubscribe via the link in your email.

Ukraine is sending ground robots into combat in record numbers to replace its soldiers in deadly roles wherever possible, from logistics missions to front-line assaults.

And while the ground robots are helping save lives, they're also changing how the Ukrainian military sustains the war as it nears the four-and-a-half-year mark and continues facing manpower challenges.

Ukrainian commanders told Business Insider that one of the benefits of uncrewed ground robots, or UGVs, is their ability to increase Kyiv's "operational endurance."

War robots don't "fatigue in the same way humans do, allowing persistent tasks such as monitoring, transport, or reconnaissance support," said Grek, a UGV company commander with the 21st Unmanned Systems "Kraken" Regiment. He used his call sign for security reasons.

The commander of a UGV unit in the Lava Regiment of the 2nd "Khartia" Corps, who goes by his call sign Mathematician, said that the main purpose of the ground robots is to decrease the number of soldiers involved in missions.

However, he said the robots have a durability advantage: they can go on more missions than a small infantry unit can, and at any time of day, too. "Without that, the Ukrainian Army cannot exist now, really. So this is definitely about durability."

Ukraine has made UGVs a priority defense investment this year. The country contracted 25,000 robots in the first half of 2026 — twice as many as in all of 2025. And Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wants 50,000 produced by the end of the year.

The investments in this technology underscore Ukraine's push to replace soldiers with robots in various combat roles, especially deadly logistics missions. Officials have praised the UGVs for their ability to save lives on the battlefield.

The robots are playing a growing role in the war. Zelenskyy said in April that UGVs had logged more than 22,000 missions since the start of the year. The figure had climbed to more than 50,000 by June.

Ukrainian UGV commanders said the aim in using the robots is to reduce the number of soldiers doing dangerous missions, but not actually remove them entirely from the war.

"Keeping humans involved in decision-making remains essential," Grek said. "UGVs are tools that support people — they can handle the most hazardous parts of a mission while humans provide judgment, control, and responsibility."

He added that the robots increase efficiency, allowing a smaller number of soldiers to control or coordinate systems that previously required more people and resources.

Ground robots are particularly valuable at the front lines, which have evolved into a miles-wide "kill zone" where any movement can draw a fatal drone strike. Ukrainian officials and soldiers have said this area is growing.

Equipped with advanced sensors and cameras, war robots provide troops farther back with greater situational awareness, allowing them to see closer to the front lines and "extending human capability," Grek said.

He said operators can "observe, deliver, recover, inspect, or support operations from a safer distance."

However, as the battlefield becomes deadlier for soldiers, it has also become riskier for robots, which move slowly and lack the same protection against drones that an armored vehicle may have.

Near the line of contact, robots may only survive five or 10 missions before they're destroyed, said Andrii Kushnierov, a platoon leader with Ukraine's 59th Assault Brigade.

Mathematician said that in some areas of the battlefield, the life of a robot may be as long as 20 missions. In his, though, it's maybe three or four. For the Ukrainians, these machine losses are worth it to keep soldiers alive.

content_html_zh:
乌克兰的地面机器人不仅在拯救生命，而且正在改变其军队承受战斗的方式

作者：Jake Epstein 您目前正在关注该作者！ 想要取消关注吗？ 通过电子邮件中的链接取消订阅。

乌克兰正在以创纪录的数量派遣地面机器人投入战斗，以尽可能取代其士兵，从后勤任务到前线突击等致命角色。

虽然地面机器人正在帮助拯救生命，但它们也正在改变乌克兰军队维持战争的方式，因为战争已接近四年半，并继续面临人力挑战。

乌克兰指挥官告诉《商业内幕》，无人地面机器人（UGV）的好处之一是它们能够提高基辅的“作战耐力”。

第 21 无人系统“海妖”团的 UGV 连指挥官格雷克说，战争机器人“不会像人类那样疲劳，可以持续执行监视、运输或侦察支持等任务”。 出于安全原因，他使用了自己的呼号。

第二“哈蒂亚”军团熔岩团一个无人车部队的指挥官（他的呼号是数学家）表示，地面机器人的主要目的是减少参与任务的士兵数量。

不过，他表示，这些机器人具有耐用性优势：它们可以比小型步兵部队执行更多的任务，而且可以在一天中的任何时间执行。 “如果没有这个，乌克兰军队现在就不可能存在，真的。 所以这绝对与耐用性有关。”

乌克兰今年已将无人地面车辆列为优先国防投资。 2026 年上半年，该国签订了 25,000 台机器人合同，是 2025 年全年的两倍。 乌克兰总统弗拉基米尔·泽连斯基 (Volodymyr Zelenskyy) 希望在今年年底前生产 50,000 辆。

对这项技术的投资凸显了乌克兰推动用机器人取代士兵来执行各种战斗任务，尤其是致命的后勤任务。 官员们赞扬无人车在战场上拯救生命的能力。

机器人在战争中发挥着越来越重要的作用。 泽连斯基 4 月份表示，自今年年初以来，UGV 已执行了超过 22,000 次任务。 到 6 月，这一数字已攀升至 50,000 多人。

乌克兰无人车指挥官表示，使用机器人的目的是减少执行危险任务的士兵数量，但实际上并没有将他们完全从战争中消除。

“让人类参与决策仍然至关重要，”格雷克说。 “UGV 是支持人类的工具——它们可以处理任务中最危险的部分，而人类则提供判断、控制和责任。”

他补充说，机器人提高了效率，允许更少数量的士兵控制或协调以前需要更多人力和资源的系统。

地面机器人在前线尤其有价值，前线已经演变成数英里宽的“杀伤区”，任何移动都可能引发致命的无人机袭击。 乌克兰官员和士兵表示，该地区正在扩大。

格雷克说，战争机器人配备了先进的传感器和摄像头，为后方的部队提供了更强的态势感知能力，使他们能够更接近前线并“扩展人类的能力”。

他说，操作员可以“在更安全的距离观察、运送、恢复、检查或支持操作”。

然而，随着战场对士兵来说变得更加致命，对于机器人来说也变得更加危险，因为机器人移动缓慢，并且缺乏装甲车可能具有的针对无人机的相同保护。

乌克兰第 59 突击旅排长安德里·库什涅罗夫 (Andrii Kushnierov) 表示，在接触线附近，机器人可能只能完成 5 到 10 次任务，然后就会被摧毁。

数学家表示，在战场的某些区域，一个机器人的寿命可能长达20次任务。 但在他的作品中，可能有三四个。 对于乌克兰人来说，为了保证士兵的生命，这些机器损失是值得的。
